text: As a ___ , I want ___ so that ___ .
user-stories.explanation: Role, want, benefit — one sentence, all three present. 'The system' is never a role; 'clean code' is a task, not a user benefit.
hints: Who benefits — a real user, not the software.

user-stories.prompt: 'As a database, I want indexes so that queries run fast' is a valid user story.

distractor.0: Stories are about users — people who use the software. A database is an implementation detail.

user-stories.explanation: False. User-story common sense: stories serve real users. System internals belong in tasks, not stories.

stakeholders-actors.prompt: Sort the restaurant scenario's people and systems

right.label: Primary actor (a person with the goal)

pairNotes.g: Regulators care deeply but never touch the use case — stakeholders, not actors.

stakeholders-actors.explanation: Actors interact; stakeholders merely care. Exactly one person carries each use-case goal; the gateway is used, the regulator only watches.

text: The ___ starts the flow; the ___ must already be true.
use-case-headers.explanation: Selecting 'plot data' triggers; being logged in pre-exists. Swapping them is the classic half-mark loss (2022 Q2.2a).

use-case-flow.instructions: Plot-data scenario, five steps. Alternate actor and system.

items.label: System lists datasets for the credentials
User picks dataset, columns and chart style
System generates, displays and saves the PNG

use-case-flow.explanation: Trigger → system lists → actor specifies → system produces → confirm. Every deviation branches to an extension, never into the main flow.

use-case-flow.prompt: 'Database network connection fails' makes a strong extension.

distractor.0: The slides' exhibit-A reject: overly-generic problems fit every system and help no designer.

use-case-flow.explanation: False. Extensions must be scenario-specific with step ID, handling and outcome — e.g. non-numeric data at step 5.

use-case-diagrams.prompt: Which case is included by 'Upload Video'?
use-case-diagrams.instructions: Click the included oval in the video-sharing diagram.
use-case-diagrams.explanation: 'Authenticate' is factored out with «include» — one shared sub-flow instead of five copies. Login-style cases are the textbook include.

nfr-validity.prompt: 'Students must finish enrolment before week 1.' Why is this not a valid NFR?
options: It governs actors, not the system — a business rule
It is actually a valid NFR

distractor.0: Its meaning is perfectly clear — clarity isn't the failure.
distractor.2: It states no reliability bound at all.
distractor.3: Check scope: who must do what?

nfr-validity.explanation: In-scope failure: the rule constrains students, not software. Business rules look like NFRs but live outside the system boundary.

nfr-validity.instructions: Run every candidate NFR through these in lecture order.

items.label: Truly non-functional, not a disguised function

nfr-validity.explanation: The Worksheet 4 Q1 verdict machine: meaning, feasibility, testability, scope, category. Fail any gate and the NFR is decoration.

performance-requirements.instructions: Name the missing fourth part of a performance requirement.
performance-requirements.explanation: Environment. 'Colour-enhance within 250 ms on a 10 MP image on an average PC' — drop the PC and the bound is untestable.

reliability-requirements.prompt: Match each system to its fitting metric

left.label: Forecast server over a cyclone season

pairNotes.vit: Continuous monitoring has no 'demands' — uptime fraction is the honest measure.

reliability-requirements.explanation: On-demand checks want per-attempt probability; continuous service wants uptime; long-running kit wants MTBF. Mismatches fail (2019 Q3 hint).

reliability-requirements.prompt: A reliability requirement should demand that the system never fails.

distractor.0: Perfection is untestable and unachievable — the worksheet says so explicitly. State an acceptable level for a stated failure class.

reliability-requirements.explanation: False. Reliability quantifies acceptable failure, never perfection — e.g. ≤1 min of lost vitals display per 24 h.

text: An average ___ shall complete a defined ___ within a ___ , with a stated ___ .
usability-requirements.explanation: User class + task + time/effort bound + success criterion. 'The system' and 'password' fail the enables-vs-obligates test — rules, not usability.

options: Users must enter a password to log in
An average user shall log in within 30 seconds unaided, 9 of 10 succeeding
The system must count logins per day

distractor.0: That obligates the user — a business rule, not an ability the system enables.
distractor.2: Counting is a function with a writable flow — an FR in disguise.

usability-requirements.explanation: Only the middle option enables (not obligates) with user, task, bound and bar. The other two fail scope and category respectively.

other-nfrs.prompt: Match each risk to its NFR family

left.label: Vitals must reach the hospital record

other-nfrs.explanation: Confidential → security; cross-system → interoperability; diverse abilities → accessibility. 2022 Q3.4(d) rewards exactly this risk-first reasoning.

srs-ieee830.prompt: Which IEEE virtue is backlog ordering in disguise?

distractor.1: Modifiability is about cheap document change, not order.
distractor.2: Traceability links requirements to sources and tests.
distractor.3: Correctness matters, but ordering is explicitly 'ranked'.

srs-ieee830.explanation: Ranked: not all requirements matter equally. The Product Owner's ordering is ranking made agile; traceability is this wiki's citation habit.

srs-ieee830.prompt: 'The system shall have a good human interface' is verifiable.

distractor.0: IEEE's own hall-of-shame example: no observation decides 'good'. Rewrite with user, task, bound, bar.

srs-ieee830.explanation: False — non-verifiable, hence invalid. Same family as 'user friendly' (2022 Q3.2b) and 'suitable for photo albums' (Worksheet 4).

ethics-theories.prompt: Match each claim to its school

left.label: 'Pull the lever: one death beats five'

ethics-theories.explanation: Duty judges the act; utility judges the outcome. The frameworks can honestly disagree — which is why engineers must deliberate explicitly.

ethics-theories.prompt: Scenario: the client leans on your estimates
ethics-theories.instructions: You and two colleagues are mid-planning-poker. The client says the bid must come down or the contract walks. Decide.

pressure.text: Estimates say 40 days; the client demands 25 and hints the contract depends on it. The team looks at you. What do you do?

options.label: Trim the cards to 25 to keep the contract
options.note: Knowingly false estimates betray the team and future users.

options.label: Refuse to change the numbers, disclose the uncertainty and offer options
options.note: Honesty plus options: the ACS stakeholder-trust response.

options.label: Say nothing and let the loudest voice decide
options.note: Silence delegates your professional judgement to pressure.

falsified.text: The project 'commits' to 25 days, overruns to 43, and the client you tried to please terminates anyway. The team absorbs unpaid overtime.
falsified.title: Numbers bent
falsified.debrief: Falsified estimates help nobody: the overrun still arrives, now compounded by broken trust. Public and stakeholder interest outranks client pressure in the ACS Code.

silent.text: Estimates drift down under pressure. Nobody owns the numbers, so nobody defends them — the same overrun, with deniability instead of integrity.
silent.title: Diffusion
silent.debrief: Diffusion of responsibility is how groups misbehave. Professionalism means owning your estimate out loud, even when it costs.

honest.text: You hold the 40-day estimate, show the breakdown, and offer scope phasing: core in 25 days, remainder next. The client pushes back. Now what?

options.label: Offer the phased scope in writing with risks stated
Concede the 40 was 'pessimistic' to smooth things over
options.note: Same falsification, slower — and now documented as yours.

phased.text: The client accepts phased delivery. The team ships the core on time; trust — the currency the ACS Code protects — survives the negotiation.
phased.title: Held the line
phased.debrief: Duty (don't lie) plus utility (a shippable core) plus code (stakeholder trust first). Frameworks converge here: honesty with options.

ethics-theories.explanation: Estimate pressure is the handout's own scenario (Example 4). The pattern generalises: disclose, document, offer options — never silently comply.
ethics-theories.source: Lecture 5 slides (PDF p. 33); ethics handout Example 4

ethics-se-professionalism.prompt: Under the ACS Code, public interest outranks loyalty to your employer or client.
ethics-se-professionalism.confirm: Health, safety, environment and stakeholder trust come first — the Code says so explicitly.
ethics-se-professionalism.explanation: True. Professionalism means the public's safety and trust constrain what any client or employer can ask of you.

midterm-study-guide.explanation: Marks density first (graphs, use cases), judgement last (ethics reasoning), then one closed-book rehearsal under time.

distractor.0: The cover says plainly: calculators are not allowed. Arithmetic must be hand-checkable — show working.

midterm-study-guide.explanation: False — closed book, no calculators, 90 minutes, 100 marks. Method marks reward shown working even with slips.

functional-requirements.prompt: Sort each sentence: function or characteristic?

left.label: 'Render them within 2 s on the lab PC'

functional-requirements.explanation: Inputs-to-outputs versus a measurable bound on that function. The worksheet's two-question test decides every case.

exam-mistakes-requirements.prompt: A use-case diagram shows the order of steps in a scenario.

distractor.0: The slides' warning slide exists precisely because this is tempting: diagrams map who-does-what, flows carry sequence.

exam-mistakes-requirements.explanation: False — that confusion is an instant mark-loser. Sequencing lives in the written flow; ovals never chain into flowcharts.

exam-mistakes-planning.prompt: Project duration equals the sum of all task durations.

distractor.0: Only the critical path's tasks sum to the duration — off-path work overlaps in time. 2022 Project A totals far more than 25 weeks of tasks.

exam-mistakes-planning.explanation: False. Duration is the longest path through the network, not the sum of everything.

exam-mistakes-nfr.prompt: POFOD is the right metric for a continuously displayed vital-signs monitor.

distractor.0: Continuous display has no discrete 'demands' — availability (uptime fraction) fits. POFOD suits on-demand checks like ticket validation.

exam-mistakes-nfr.explanation: False — the classic metric mismatch. Match the metric to the usage pattern or the requirement is nonsense.
